name: Online feature store for ranking / recsys
category: Adjacent — generic online feature store role (ranking slice)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Online feature store, ranking / recsys slice — beava as the inference-time feature backend for the second-stage (re-rank) of a search / feed / recommendation pipeline, sitting between an upstream retrieval/ANN stage and a downstream tabular or neural scorer.
domain_fit.one_line_definition: An ML platform team must serve, in a single batched call inside a ~100–200 ms request budget, every behavioural and popularity feature needed by the re-rank scorer for one user against the 50–500 candidate items returned by retrieval, while events keep streaming in at full ingest rate.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete JTBDs distinguish 18b from 18a (the fraud/risk classifier slice of the online FS role) and from 6 (full personalization platform): (1) Serve a single batched `get_features(user_id, [item_id_1 ... item_id_N], feature_set)` inside the re-rank RPC so the scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / DLRM / cross-encoder) gets per-user, per-item and per-(user, item-attribute) signals without making N round-trips — this is the canonical 'online FS at ranking' workload that Tecton, Chalk, Hopsworks, Feast and Fennel all motivate themselves on. (2) Keep per-item velocity / popularity counters fresh in seconds (clicks/min, CTR, add-to-cart rate, unique-viewers/min) so newly-listed items, livestreams or flash-sale SKUs get a usable cold-start signal in the same session — Pinterest, Whatnot and TikTok Shop publicly cite multi-minute lag as the failure mode that justified building real-time feature infra. (3) Provide a single feature definition surface that the upstream materialization job can replay against historical events to produce training data — the 'compute features once, serve them online and offline' contract that distinguishes a feature store from a vanilla KV cache. Beava covers (1) and (2) natively; (3) is an open engineering gap.
domain_fit.event_shapes: The same event vocabulary as item 6, but viewed through the FS-role lens: impression {ts, user_id, item_id, surface, position, query?, request_id}, click {ts, user_id, item_id, surface, position, request_id}, dwell {ts, user_id, item_id, dwell_ms}, add_to_cart {ts, user_id, sku, price, qty}, favorite {ts, user_id, item_id}, purchase {ts, user_id, order_id, sku, price, qty, seller_id, category, brand}, livestream_join / leave / dwell {ts, user_id, show_id, duration_ms}, search_query {ts, user_id, q_hash}, item_listed / item_updated {ts, item_id, seller_id, category, price}. Beava's existing python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ ships PageView / AddToCart / Purchase records keyed on user_id and sku (verified by reading schema.json), which is exactly the recsys event shape; impression / dwell / click are natural extensions to add as `@bv.event` schemas.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Per-entity aggregations using beava `@bv.table(key=...)` primitives, organized by the grain the ranker queries: USER grain → count(click, 1m/10m/1h/24h), count(add_to_cart, 24h), count(purchase, 30d), velocity(click, 1m), distribution(dwell_ms, 1h), n_unique(category_id, 7d), sum(purchase_amount, 7d/30d), last_n(item_id, n=50) for last-viewed / last-clicked streams; ITEM grain → count(impression, 1m/10m/1h), count(click, 1m/10m/1h), CTR rolling, count(add_to_cart, 1h), count(purchase, 1h/24h), distribution(dwell_ms, 1h), n_unique(user_id, 1h) (HLL-friendly); (USER, CATEGORY) and (USER, SELLER) compound keys → count(click, 7d/30d), affinity ratio, recency-decayed dwell, time-since-last-interaction; SHOW grain (livestreams) → count(join, 1m), distribution(dwell_ms, current-session), n_unique(user_id, 1m), velocity(chat, 1m). Both exact (counters, sums, last-N) and approximate (HLL/CMS/T-Digest) primitives have legitimate roles — ranking is tolerant of 1–2 % HLL/CMS error on high-cardinality grains.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Parallel keys read in a single ranking call: user_id (1 row), item_id / sku / show_id (50–500 rows fanned out), and the compound (user_id, category_id) / (user_id, seller_id) / (user_id, brand_id) pairs for the same fan-out. Secondary grains used as context features but not fanned out per candidate: session_id, query_hash, seller_id (in aggregate), creator_id.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate (1m, 5m, 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d for user-side; 1m, 10m, 1h for item-side popularity). Session windows are critical for in-session re-ranking (per browse session, per livestream). Tumbling windows show up only for daily reporting / offline-online consistency checks. Approximate primitives (HLL for per-item unique-viewers, CMS for high-cardinality counts, T-Digest for dwell distributions) are first-class for ranking — the model is robust to small approximation error and that error is invisible compared to model variance. Exactness IS desired for the offline materialization that produces training labels, which is the consistency story.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once with idempotent counters keyed on event_id or (user_id, item_id, ts) is sufficient at ranking time. Unlike ad-cap (3) or AML (8) or usage-billing (14b), a double-counted click does not change the ranking score appreciably. Strict exactly-once is NOT required for the online serving path; it IS desirable for the offline training-data materialization to avoid label leakage.

technical_fit.latency_budget: End-to-end ranking RPC budget is 100–200 ms (Netflix sub-100 ms personalization; Whatnot on Chalk P99 ~100 ms and ~150 ms end-to-end with 1 MB+ payloads; Apartment List on Chalk sub-5 ms feature retrieval; Tecton documents sub-10 ms p99 managed feature serving and sub-25 ms Redis-backed SLO; Hopsworks/RonDB 1.93 ms avg / 3 ms p99 for 100-row batch lookups; Metarank 10–20 ms reranking p99 on top of Redis). The feature-fetch sub-budget is typically 5–30 ms because model inference itself consumes 30–80 ms. Beava's published sub-millisecond TCP get / batch_get fits inside that envelope for small fan-outs; the open empirical question is the (1 user × ~30 features) + (200 items × ~30 features) shape at p99.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Seconds, not sub-second. This is the key distinction from item 18a (fraud / risk classifier slice), which requires sub-second freshness or it degrades to zero-velocity counters and lets the fraudster through. Recsys is tolerant: tens of seconds of lag on item-velocity counters is recoverable (the candidate set itself has retrieval-stage lag baked in), and per-user behavioural profile features can be minutes stale without measurable model regression. Pinterest reports a 10 s p99 end-to-end signal-to-serving lag in production. Beava's push-on-event architecture delivers single-digit-ms feature staleness, which overshoots the SLA — useful headroom rather than required precision.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Read-dominated and bursty. A single ranking call multiplies into 50–500 candidate fan-outs, each pulling 5–30 features per item plus 5–30 user-side features and 5–10 compound-key features. Mid-size marketplace QPS 1k–10k ranking requests/sec produces 100k–5M feature reads/sec at the FS interface. Published references: DoorDash >1M predictions/sec and >20M feature reads/sec on their Redis-based store (peak >10M reads/sec, ~1,000 lookups per prediction); Whatnot via Chalk 300M+ features/sec; Tecton+Redis 100k+ QPS sustained; Swiggy on ElastiCache 50M QPS; Hopsworks/RonDB 100M key lookups/sec via REST. Beava's published 684k EPS (TCP+msgpack+parallel=16, single Apple-M4 core) is the WRITE-side ingest figure; the corresponding batched-read figure for the (1 user × 200 items × 30 features) fan-out has not been publicly benchmarked. [uncertain] beava's published batch_get throughput at recsys-shape fan-out.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Strongly read-heavy at inference time, typically 10:1 to 100:1 read:write — the opposite of the fraud (1a–1c) and ad-tech (3, 4) shapes. One user event produces one or a few writes; each ranking decision triggers dozens-to-hundreds of batched reads. DoorDash and Tecton both call this fan-out asymmetry the dominant sizing factor for the online FS role at ranking. This is also distinct from 18a, which is closer to balanced (1 transaction → 1 decision → 20–100 features, no fan-out across candidates).
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order of magnitude per buyer: ~10M MAU × ~5 grains (user, item, (user, cat), (user, seller), session) × ~30–80 features × ~16–64 bytes per counter (more for last-N item lists and T-Digest distributions) ≈ 50–200 GB hot state for a mid-sized marketplace — at the upper edge of a single beava box. Whatnot-class global live commerce (hundreds of millions of impressions/day) and DoorDash-class platforms (billions of feature-value pairs) push into multi-TB and exceed the single-binary in-memory ceiling. Beava's in-memory-only model fits the long-tail of mid-sized marketplaces and ML teams who do not yet need multi-node sharding.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Mixed, with one explosive axis: user_id slowly-growing (MAU), category_id / brand_id / seller_id bounded-ish, item_id (SKU, listing, livestream show) unbounded and explosive — millions to billions across a global marketplace. (user, item) pair grain is the cardinality killer and is generally NOT materialized; the ranker assembles it at query time from user-side and item-side rows. Last-N item lists per user are bounded (N=20–100). HLL/CMS for high-cardinality unique-counter features keeps memory tractable.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed TTLs by grain: in-session last-N lists minutes-to-hours; user behavioural profile 30–90 days rolling; long-term affinity 6–12 months; per-item popularity 1m–24h rolling; livestream show stats the lifetime of the show (minutes-to-hours) then archived. Training-data interaction logs live for years — but in the warehouse, not in beava.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: Highly fan-out shape: ~5–30 user-side features × 1 user + ~10–50 per-item features × 50–500 candidates + ~5–10 (user, item-attribute) compound features × 50–500 + ~5–10 contextual features. Total feature reads per ranking call: roughly 1,000–25,000 (Whatnot via Chalk reports 'tens of thousands of features' per request with 1 MB+ payloads; DoorDash reports ~1,000 feature lookups per prediction). Qualitatively different from item 18a (one decision, 20–100 features, no candidate fan-out).
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe is sufficient. Loss of recent in-session signals during a crash is recoverable: the session itself usually short-circuits, the long-term aggregates can be replayed from the upstream event bus, and the ranker degrades gracefully when fresh features are missing (back-off to staler or coarser features). Regulator-grade durability is NOT required for ranking — distinct from item 8 (AML) or 14b (usage-based billing). Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot exceeds the bar.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional fits a single-region marketplace, a mid-size e-commerce ranking team, or a single-tenant SaaS personalization product cleanly. Multi-region active-active for global marketplaces (Whatnot / Pinterest / DoorDash scale) is NOT supported in beava v0 — no in-process sharding, no cross-region replication, no read-replicas. Buyers operating a global live-commerce platform would need an external sharding layer or a multi-node successor; the FS-role 18b shape is sensitive to this because the data-residency story (per-region user state) is often a customer requirement.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Primary buyer: the ML platform team (Head of ML Platform, Director of Search & Recommendations, Staff ML Engineer on the ranking team) at marketplaces, content / media platforms, live-commerce, e-commerce retailers, news aggregators. Secondary buyer: the data platform / streaming infra team that owns the upstream event bus and would otherwise spin up Flink + Redis to do the same job. Tertiary buyer: the growth / experimentation team that owns the feed and ranking experiments and is feature-engineering-bottlenecked. Distinct from item 18a, where the buyer is the fraud / risk team and the deployment lives in-line with auth or checkout.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large. Real-time online feature stores raised significant capital in the 2022–2025 window — Tecton, Chalk, Hopsworks, Featureform, Fennel (acquired by Databricks April 2025, Rust-based real-time engine, customers in personalized ranking and marketplace recommendations). Public lighthouse references: DoorDash (>1M predictions/sec store ranking, >20M feature reads/sec, ~1,000 features per prediction), Whatnot on Chalk (300M+ features/sec, P99 100 ms, $3B+ live sales), Apartment List on Chalk (sub-5 ms ranking feature retrieval), Instacart Griffin 2.0 (Flink + internal store, Ray for training), Pinterest Manas/TransAct (1.2M user-action events/sec, 10 s p99 signal-to-serving, +11 % Homefeed engagement from real-time sequence features), Sony PlayStation on Aerospike, Swiggy on ElastiCache (50M QPS), Meesho XGBoost-to-DL ranking, Myntra on Aerospike, Meta DLRMv3 (80 ms p99 server-scenario benchmark). Livestream commerce is the fastest-growing slice (~33.9 % CAGR; TikTok Shop >$100M U.S. Black Friday 2024 across 30k+ livestream sessions); horizontal recsys is much larger (Netflix attributes 80 %+ of watch time to recommendations, YouTube ~70 %, Spotify ~60 %). [uncertain] precise revenue for Tecton / Chalk / Hopsworks — most are private.
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Three forces: (1) Freshness gap — batch-trained, batch-served models are visibly stale for live commerce (a livestream that started 60 seconds ago has zero batch features) and increasingly inadequate for session-level personalization even in traditional e-commerce. Pinterest, Whatnot, TikTok Shop, Instacart have all publicly cited multi-minute lag as the trigger to build real-time feature infra. (2) Compute economics — running a 'compute features at request time in Spark / on the application server' architecture is expensive and slow; collapsing it to a pushed-counter feature server is materially cheaper, especially when one ranking call fans out to hundreds of candidates. (3) Org pull / internal precedent — DoorDash, Instacart, Whatnot, Apartment List, Swiggy, Pinterest, Myntra, Sony PlayStation have all published case studies in the past 2–3 years, which gives a buyer's ML platform team internal political cover to make the same investment.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Light relative to fraud / AML / KYC / billing. GDPR / CCPA apply because user_id / session_id / device_id are personal data; right-to-erasure requires per-user delete that propagates through derived aggregates (beava's per-entity TTL story partially covers this). EU DSA / DMA require ranking-transparency for very large platforms but the obligation is documentation, not feature storage. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for enterprise customers buying the platform that uses the feature store. No PCI / FFIEC / HIPAA exposure typically. The audit pressure on this domain is materially lower than on 18a (fraud / risk), 8 (AML), or 14b (billing).
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A runnable per-user last-N-viewed-SKU and per-item rolling-CTR demo can stand up on beava in roughly a day: the repo already ships python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ with PageView / AddToCart / Purchase events keyed on user_id and sku, which is the recsys event shape. A realistic 30–80-feature per-user × per-item × per-(user, category) ranking-feature rig integrated against a real impression / click stream is a 1–2 week effort. Replicating a Whatnot-class production ranking platform is a multi-quarter project even with beava as the substrate. This positions 18b as an excellent 'design partner with one ML platform team' wedge rather than a commodity SaaS play.

competition.incumbents: Three layers. (a) Dedicated real-time feature stores: Tecton (Spark/Flink materialization + low-latency online store; sub-10 ms p99 served features; Redis Enterprise reported 3x faster and 14x cheaper than DynamoDB in their benchmarks), Chalk (real-time feature engine; Whatnot 300M+ features/sec; Apartment List sub-5 ms; the explicit 'search & ranking' marketed use case), Hopsworks (RonDB-backed; 100M key lookups/sec via REST, 1.93 ms avg / 3 ms p99 for 100-row batches; SIGMOD 2024 paper claims 10x lower p99 vs SageMaker / Vertex), Feast (open-source, Redis or DynamoDB online store; the BYO-online-store reference), Fennel (Rust real-time engine, Databricks acquisition April 2025, Upwork / Cricut among published customers, explicit 'personalized ranking and marketplace recommendations' use cases), Featureform (virtual feature store, orchestrates over Snowflake/Databricks + Redis online), AWS SageMaker Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store, Databricks Feature Store. (b) Online KV stores used to build feature stores in-house: Redis / managed Redis / Redis Enterprise / ElastiCache (DoorDash, Instacart, Swiggy, GoJek, Feast default), Aerospike (Sony PlayStation, Adobe, Criteo, Wayfair, Myntra), DynamoDB, ScyllaDB, RonDB, KeyDB, Dragonfly. (c) Ranking-service products that bundle the FS role with a scorer: Metarank (open-source learn-to-rank, Redis-backed state, 10–20 ms p99 reranking, single-batch feature fetch design), Recombee, Algolia AI Recommendations, Amazon Personalize, Google Recommendations AI. Beava competes most directly with the (Redis or Aerospike) + (Flink or Spark Real-Time Mode) two-box pattern by collapsing it into a single binary; against Tecton / Chalk / Hopsworks it competes on ops surface area (single binary, no Kafka required) and licensing (Apache-2.0, no open-core split).
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific personalization-as-a-product vendors that buyers would otherwise procure black-box: Dynamic Yield, Adobe Target, Algolia AI Recommendations, Bloomreach, Recombee, Amazon Personalize, Google Recommendations AI, Coveo, Constructor.io, Nosto, Klevu. These compete with the buyer's own ranking team rather than with beava; beava is the infrastructure layer a buyer who is building their own ranking stack would use. For the FS-role slice specifically, the closest direct competitor is the (Chalk / Tecton / Hopsworks managed cloud) bundle plus the in-house (Feast + Redis + Flink) pattern.
competition.beava_differentiator: Six concrete differentiators relevant to the 18b slice: (1) Single binary — no Kafka + Flink + Redis + feature-store ETL chain; the lowest-ops-surface option for an ML platform team that does not want to run a streaming engine. (2) 50+ first-class aggregation primitives mapped exactly to the shape ranking features take on top of Redis Lua / Aerospike UDFs (counters, velocities, distributions, last-N lists, rates). (3) Push-on-event ingestion over HTTP/JSON :8080 and framed TCP :8081 (JSON or msgpack) — Kafka is optional, not required, which is a wedge against Tecton / Feast / Hopsworks pipelines that assume a Kafka stream. Many marketplace event streams are already HTTP webhooks or mobile-SDK direct push. (4) Apache-2.0, no open-core enterprise edition — material differentiator against Tecton (managed-only), Chalk (managed-only), Hopsworks (open-core with Enterprise feature gates). (5) batch_get / get-many semantics map naturally to the ranking fan-out shape (one call, many features, many entities). (6) Published 684k EPS sustained on a single core demonstrates the write path is not the bottleneck, freeing the buyer to focus on read-side tuning; this is competitive with Aerospike-class single-node throughput and well above what most teams achieve with Redis Lua scripts. The 'Redis for stateful streaming features, with 50+ aggregation primitives' positioning lands directly in this slice.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that block production ranking deployments today: (1) No TLS / no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — ML platform teams in cloud VPCs will demand mTLS or at minimum bearer-token auth before letting beava sit next to a ranking service. Hard blocker for procurement. (2) No in-process sharding / consistent hashing across multiple beava instances — Whatnot / DoorDash / Instacart-class state cannot fit on one box; the buyer must vertically scale and accept a single point of failure. (3) No cross-region replication or read-replicas — global marketplaces with multi-region ranking paths cannot use beava as the source of truth. (4) Read-amplification story for batch_get with 50–500 candidate fan-out × 30 features per item is unproven publicly; the 684k EPS headline is the write-side number, not the recsys-shape batched-read number. The buyer will require a published p99 at this fan-out shape. (5) No point-in-time-correct offline materialization to produce training data from the same feature definitions — this is the headline 'consistency' feature Hopsworks, Tecton, Chalk, Fennel and Featureform sell, and its absence makes beava a 'fast online cache' rather than a full feature store in the procurement sense. (6) No vector / ANN index (modern two-tower retrieval needs an ANN sidecar — Vespa, Milvus, Vald, Aerospike Vector Search, Redis Search); beava is feature-serving, not candidate-retrieval. (7) No native embedding storage / high-dimensional vector primitives. (8) No multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs — a SaaS personalization vendor cannot safely host multiple customers on one box. (9) Refuse-on-network-FS is the right invariant for durability but constrains deployment topologies (cannot back the snapshot file on EFS / Azure Files). (10) No triggers — useful for trending-now and cold-start surfacing.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers in 18b are heterogeneous: Kafka / Kinesis for large marketplaces (Whatnot, DoorDash, Instacart, Pinterest), the application server's own click / impression / view webhook (HTTP push, common in mid-size shops), mobile SDK direct push (for in-app dwell and scroll), gRPC from a ranking-side service, Flink / Spark Real-Time Mode jobs that pre-aggregate features. Beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 plus framed-TCP :8081 (JSON or msgpack) maps cleanly to the webhook and mobile-SDK paths. A thin Kafka / Kinesis consumer is required for the streaming-bus paths and is not shipped in v0 — a documented sidecar pattern would close the gap. Downstream consumers are the ranker (XGBoost / LightGBM / DLRM / two-tower / cross-encoder / transformer) pulling features via batch_get inside the ranking RPC, optionally followed by a business-rules layer for diversity / freshness / business constraints.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: ML scorer dominates. Production stacks are XGBoost / LightGBM for tabular re-ranking (Meesho, DoorDash, Instacart historically), DLRM-class deep recommender models (Meta, DLRMv3 MLPerf benchmark, 80 ms p99 server-scenario target), two-tower retrieval + neural re-rankers (Whatnot, Pinterest, TikTok Shop), plus transformer-based sequence models (Pinterest TransAct V2 with 16k+ lifelong user actions). Cross-encoder rerankers are used for the head queries on search surfaces. Rules engines appear only for hard business constraints (don't show this seller to this user, freshness cap, diversity quota). Beava sits under the ML scorer and is largely scorer-agnostic — the contract is `batch_get(entity_ids, feature_names) -> dense vector`.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users running this use case yet. Comparable published references that legitimise the FS-role-at-ranking shape: DoorDash on Redis ElastiCache (store ranking >1M predictions/sec, ~1,000 feature lookups per prediction, >20M feature reads/sec, 40 % read-latency improvement and 2.85x CPU reduction after optimization), Whatnot on Chalk (300M+ features/sec, P99 100 ms, end-to-end 150 ms with 1 MB+ payloads, thousands of livestreams scored per session, cold-start <1 h vs prior 24 h), Apartment List on Chalk (sub-5 ms feature retrieval, weeks-to-days model deployment cycle), Instacart Griffin 2.0 (Flink-based real-time features + Ray training + REST control plane), Pinterest Manas + TransAct V2 (1.2M user-action events/sec ingest, 10 s p99 signal-to-serving lag, 75–81 % lower model p99 after optimization, +11 % Homefeed engagement / -10 % hide volume from real-time sequence features), Sony PlayStation on Aerospike (online FS for personalization, Spark for offline materialization, Kafka delivery to scorers), Swiggy on ElastiCache (50M QPS reported), Myntra on Aerospike (re-ranking, feature lookup was the bottleneck), Meesho on XGBoost-to-DL ranking (sub-5 ms per-feature constraint), Meta DLRMv3 MLPerf (80 ms p99 server-scenario target with hierarchical parameter servers and streaming aggregations), Hopsworks SIGMOD 2024 benchmark (10x lower p99 vs SageMaker / Vertex, 1.93 ms avg / 3 ms p99 for 100-row batches), Fennel customers (Upwork, Cricut, personalized ranking and marketplace recommendations explicitly listed). [uncertain] specific revenue / GTV numbers for Tecton / Chalk / Hopsworks tiers.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] No specific beava Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on the 18b FS-role slice were located through public web search. The repo ships python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ (PageView / AddToCart / Purchase, keyed on user_id and sku) and the beava-website .planning notes reference YC application materials that mention recsys / personalization as one of the candidate domains, but external community traction in the recsys-FS-role slice specifically has not been verified.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: Partial. /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ ships PageView, AddToCart and Purchase events keyed on user_id / sku (verified by reading schema.json), which is the canonical recsys event shape and a direct stepping-stone for an 18b demo. No explicit per-item rolling-popularity, per-(user, category) affinity, or ranking-shaped batch_get demo was found. crates/beava-bench/configs/ contains fraud-team.json, geo.json, large.json, medium.json, phase8.json, large-with-sketches.json and similar — no recsys-shaped workload config was found. A 'recsys-rerank' bench config plus a ranking demo in examples/ would close the most visible gap.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Passive load. The 18b slice has no active adversary in the fraud / anti-cheat sense — no one is attacking the feature server to make it return wrong values. Feature drift is driven by genuine user-behaviour shifts (seasonality, viral events, holiday spikes), so feature-staleness tolerances are more forgiving than in fraud (18a). The exception is integrity / ranking-manipulation (sellers gaming popularity counters, click farms inflating CTR), which exists but is handled by separate trust-and-safety logic upstream, not by the feature store.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: Beava is the wrong tool for: (1) Candidate retrieval / first-stage narrowing from millions to thousands — that is an ANN / vector-index problem (Vespa, Milvus, Vald, Aerospike Vector Search, Redis Search, pgvector) and is explicitly the layer 18b sits ABOVE, not the layer beava replaces. (2) Long historical training-data materialization with point-in-time correctness — that belongs in a warehouse (Snowflake Dynamic Tables, Databricks Delta, BigQuery) with Tecton / Hopsworks / Feast / Fennel handling the offline-online sync. (3) Embedding storage and similarity search — beava primitives are scalar aggregations keyed on a primary key, not high-dimensional vectors. (4) Joins across entities at query time — (user × item) joins are computed at the ranker, not in the feature store. (5) Cross-region active-active state for global ranking platforms in v0. (6) Multi-tenant SaaS personalization platforms hosting many customers on one box (no namespace ACLs, no per-tenant isolation). (7) Replacement for a full feature-platform stack — beava is the online-serving + ingest layer, not a model registry, training-job runner, or experiment system.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship for this domain, in rough priority order: (1) TLS + authentication (mTLS or bearer-token) on :8080/:8081 — hard blocker for any production ML platform team to put beava in their VPC. (2) Published batch_get benchmark for the recsys-shape fan-out — (1 user × ~30 user-features) + (200 items × ~30 item-features) + (200 pairs × ~5 pair-features), target p99 < 5 ms for the feature-fetch sub-budget. A `crates/beava-bench/configs/recsys-rerank.json` workload definition is the natural artefact. (3) Native last-N list primitive (LPUSH/LTRIM-like behaviour) for recently-viewed / recently-clicked / recently-purchased streams; needs to be verified against the published 50+ primitives. (4) In-process sharding / consistent hashing across multiple beava instances for horizontal scaling beyond a single box. (5) Point-in-time correctness story — an offline materialization path that replays the same `@bv.table` aggregation primitives over a historical event log and produces training data with as-of joins. This is the single biggest functional gap against Tecton / Hopsworks / Chalk / Fennel for procurement evaluators. (6) Multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs for SaaS deployments. (7) Right-to-erasure helper (per-entity delete that propagates through all derived aggregates) — covers GDPR / CCPA in this domain. (8) Kafka / Kinesis consumer sidecar (documented integration pattern is acceptable; native consumer is not v0 priority). (9) Approximate-aggregation primitives (HLL, CMS, T-Digest) for high-cardinality unique-viewer / dwell-distribution features — partially shipped per the 50+ primitives claim but needs to be made discoverable. (10) Optional vector / embedding sidecar contract — beava itself probably should not become an ANN index, but a documented integration with Vespa / Milvus / Aerospike Vector Search closes the candidate-retrieval gap for buyers building an end-to-end ranking stack. (11) Triggers / 'fire when item velocity exceeds threshold' — enables trending-now widgets and real-time cold-start surfacing. (12) Multi-region / cross-region replication for global ranking platforms (post-v1, large effort).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Optional but useful. Pure feature serving is sufficient for the core re-rank job. Triggers (fire when an item's velocity crosses a threshold, fire when a user enters a new high-affinity category) would enable trending-now widgets, real-time cold-start surfacing, and online A/B-test instrumentation, but a ranker that polls per request also works and is the common pattern in DoorDash, Apartment List, Whatnot.
